original_summary: Mariáš is a Czech three-player trick-taking game with a 32-card deck. One declarer, who chooses trump and takes a talon, plays 10 tricks against two defenders in partnership. Players must follow suit, head the trick and trump when void. Aces and Tens count 10 each, the last trick counts 10, and a marriage (King and Ober of one suit) is worth 20 or 40. Flek doubling, Hearts doubling and special contracts set the stakes.

review.evidence: In the original, no simple policy wins. Always passing never earns points as declarer and depends on others failing. Always declaring high loses badly with weak hands. The seat advantage of being eldest is offset because everyone holds that seat in turn. The previous variation kept this, but its duplicate rotation made deals 2 and 3 almost perfect information.

Card play, counting the Aces and Tens, choosing when to declare and Flek decisions all separate strong players from weak ones. The card deal adds variance over a single deal, but over several deals the bidding lets players avoid bad hands and punish overbids.

Inferring hidden cards from play, defenders signalling to each other, and judging contract levels against an unknown talon have a high skill ceiling. A weak player still scores by defending or by declaring a strong hand.

In the original, hands and the talon are hidden, so play depends on inferring card locations and the declarer's intent. In the previous variation, after deal 1 every card was public, so deals 2 and 3 had little or nothing left to infer. That is the flaw this revision fixes.

Trick winners, card points, whether the contract is made and the stake are all arithmetic. Only the legality of a card needs a rule check, and with the original 'always head the trick' rule that check is mechanical.

The full original is too large for the limits: 32 cards, 10 tricks, talon exchange, marriages, four special contracts and redoubles. The previous variation went over 20 steps and 20 attributes. It also had a rule gap when trump is led.

problems: Rule gap when trump is led: the previous duty to beat the trick applied only 'if no trump has been played', so it was unclear whether a player must overtake in a trump-led trick.
Complexity was undercounted: the flat step list for the bidding round plus the trick rounds came to about 21-24 steps, attributes went over 20, and the single sequential play step was never stated.

Hidden information was overstated: with duplicate rotation, after deal 1 all 24 cards were public, so deal 2 hid only a 50/50 rotation (revealed in the first trick) and deal 3 was perfect information.
The full original (32 cards, talon exchange, marriages, special contracts, redouble) does not fit the step and choice limits.
The previous variation's partner exception to the overtaking duty added a judgment call that is not in the original and invited conflicting rulings.

changes.what: Use the original Mariáš heading rule, worded so that it covers every lead. If the currently winning card is of the suit led (including when trump is led), a player who follows suit must play a higher card of that suit if able. A player void in the led suit must trump and must beat any trump already played if able. This duty applies whoever is winning, partner or not.
changes.why: One unambiguous rule that a referee can check mechanically, and it matches the original game.
changes.fixes: Rule gap when trump is led: the previous duty to beat the trick applied only 'if no trump has been played', so it was unclear whether a player must overtake in a trump-led trick.

changes.what: Drop the partner exception to the duty to overtake or trump.
changes.why: It removes a judgment call and restores the original's 'must head' rule.
changes.fixes: The previous variation's partner exception to the overtaking duty added a judgment call that is not in the original and invited conflicting rulings.

changes.what: Replace duplicate rotation with a fresh shuffle every deal. Deal 7 cards to each seat and leave a 3-card talon that is never seen and never played.
changes.why: Every deal now has real hidden hands, and the hidden talon makes the points available uncertain. Bidding becomes a risk judgment and card counting becomes inference rather than bookkeeping.
changes.fixes: Hidden information was overstated: with duplicate rotation, after deal 1 all 24 cards were public, so deal 2 hid only a 50/50 rotation (revealed in the first trick) and deal 3 was perfect information.

changes.what: Play 5 deals of 8 rounds (1 bidding round plus 7 tricks), 40 rounds in total. Bid ties go to the tied player with the lowest match score, then to seat order from the eldest.
changes.why: More deals average out the luck that fresh shuffles bring back. Breaking ties by lowest score first neutralises the small advantage of being eldest twice in 5 deals.
changes.fixes: Hidden information was overstated: with duplicate rotation, after deal 1 all 24 cards were public, so deal 2 hid only a 50/50 rotation (revealed in the first trick) and deal 3 was perfect information.

changes.what: Declare a flat step list of 19 steps with `when` gates. Use one sequential choice step for all three card plays in a trick. Keep the hands and talon in engine hidden hands, and take bids directly from the poll. This gives 16 attributes.
changes.why: Stays inside the limits of 20 steps, 4 choice steps and 20 attributes.
changes.fixes: Complexity was undercounted: the flat step list for the bidding round plus the trick rounds came to about 21-24 steps, attributes went over 20, and the single sequential play step was never stated.

changes.what: Keep the cut-down deck (24 cards, A to 9), leave out marriages, talon exchange and special contracts, and keep Flek (no redouble) and Hearts doubling.
changes.why: Keeps the core of declarer against two defenders, contract levels and doubling while fitting the 4 choice steps.
changes.fixes: The full original (32 cards, talon exchange, marriages, special contracts, redouble) does not fit the step and choice limits.

keeps: Three players: one declarer against two defenders in a partnership.
Mariáš card ranking A, 10, K, O, U, 9 and the Czech suits.
Aces and Tens worth 10 points each, plus 10 for the last trick.
The original duties to follow suit, head the trick and trump when void.
The declarer chooses trump, and Hearts trump doubles the stakes.
Flek: defenders can double the stake.
A contract is made or failed against a card-point threshold; the declarer wins or loses double what each defender pays or receives.

recommendation.reason: The core of Mariáš (bidding against hidden hands, declarer against a partnership, counting points) fits the limits once cut to 24 cards and 7 tricks, with a hidden talon keeping every deal a game of inference.

variation.name: Mini Mariáš with Hidden Talon
variation.summary: A five-deal, three-player Mariáš. Each deal is freshly shuffled with a 3-card hidden talon. Players bid a contract of 40, 50 or 60 card points, the declarer picks trump, defenders may Flek, and 7 tricks are played under the original must-follow, must-head, must-trump rules.
variation.rules:
DECK: 24 cards in four suits (Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns). Each suit has A, 10, K, O (Ober), U (Unter) and 9, ranking high to low A, 10, K, O, U, 9. Card points: each Ace 10, each Ten 10, all other cards 0. The side that wins the last (7th) trick of a deal also gets 10. At most 90 card points are available in a deal; fewer if Aces or Tens lie in the talon.

SEATS AND MATCH: Seats 1, 2 and 3. Seat order runs 1, 2, 3, 1 and so on. The match has 5 deals of 8 rounds each, 40 rounds in total. The eldest is Seat 1 in deal 1, Seat 2 in deal 2, Seat 3 in deal 3, Seat 1 in deal 4 and Seat 2 in deal 5. Match scores start at 0 and are public. There is no talk at any time. Hands are shown to their owner sorted by suit (Hearts, Bells, Leaves, Acorns), then by rank from high to low.

ROUND 1 OF EACH DEAL (DEAL AND BID):
(a) Shuffle all 24 cards. Deal 7 cards privately to each seat. The remaining 3 cards are the talon. The talon is face down, is never played and is never shown to anyone, including at the end of the deal. Each player sees only their own hand.
(b) All three players bid at the same time without seeing the other bids. The options are PASS, 40, 50 or 60.
(c) If all three pass, the deal is not played. Rounds 2-8 of this deal are skipped with no plays and no scoring.
(d) Otherwise the highest bid wins and that player is the declarer. If several players tie for the highest bid, it goes to the tied player with the lowest match score. If they are still tied, it goes to the tied player who comes first in seat order starting from the eldest.
(e) The declarer chooses trump: Hearts, Bells, Leaves or Acorns.
(f) The declarer, the contract (the winning bid) and trump are announced. The other two players are the defenders, and their card points this deal are pooled together.
(g) Flek: the two defenders each choose FLEK or NO at the same time. Both choices are announced.
(h) Stake V: start at 1 for a 40 contract, 2 for 50 and 4 for 60. Double V if trump is Hearts. Double V again if at least one defender chose FLEK. V is announced.

ROUNDS 2-8 OF EACH DEAL (ONE TRICK PER ROUND):
(a) The declarer leads in round 2. In later rounds, the winner of the previous trick leads. The leader plays any card from their hand face up. Then the next player in seat order plays, then the third. Each card is shown to everyone as it is played.
(b) LEGAL CARDS. The 'currently winning card' is the card that would win the trick right now under rule (c). The following rules apply to every player, whoever is currently winning.
  1. If you hold a card of the suit led, you must play a card of that suit. If the currently winning card is of the suit led, you must play a higher card of that suit if you have one. This includes the case where trump was led. If the currently winning card is a trump and the suit led is not trump, any card of the suit led is legal.
  2. If you hold no card of the suit led but hold a trump, you must play a trump. If a trump has already been played in this trick, you must play a higher trump than the highest one played if you have one; otherwise any trump.
  3. If you hold neither the suit led nor a trump, you may play any card.
(c) The trick is won by the highest trump in it. If it contains no trump, it is won by the highest card of the suit led.
(d) The trick's card points go to the declarer if the declarer won it, or to the defenders' pooled total if either defender won it. In round 8 the last-trick 10 also goes to the side that won the trick. Running totals are announced.
(e) The trick winner leads the next round.

SCORING AT THE END OF ROUND 8 (only if the deal was played): the contract is made if the declarer's card points are at least the contract (40, 50 or 60).
- Made: the declarer gains 2V and each defender loses V.
- Failed: the declarer loses 2V and each defender gains V.
Match scores are announced.

END: the game ends after round 40.
variation.objective: After round 40, the player with the highest match score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest score, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect:
Every deal is a fresh hidden-information problem. Bidders must judge their hand against two unseen hands and an unseen talon that may hold up to 30 card points. Defenders must infer the declarer's holdings from the bid and trump choice, and Flek only when they read the contract as shaky. Card play rewards counting the eight Aces and Tens and inferring where the missing ones are, including whether they are in the talon. The always-head rule removes rule ambiguity.

Simple policies lose. Always passing never earns as declarer, and against competent declarers who make their contracts it bleeds V per deal. Always bidding 60 fails with weak hands at a stake of 4-16 and loses heavily. Always choosing FLEK doubles losses against strong declarers. Random play loses to counting.

Luck from the deal is reduced by the bidding choice (a weak hand can pass and defend), by five deals, and by the lowest-score tie-break.

Talk is omitted. The defenders share an interest and would coordinate trivially, and in-play signalling through cards is the intended channel. The game is zero-sum and has no endgame unravelling problem, because it is not a cooperation game.

balanced.evidence:
Point arithmetic checks out. The four Aces and four Tens are 80 points, plus 10 for the last (8th) trick, giving 90. Each hand of 8 cards plays 8 tricks, which are rounds 2-9.

Scoring is zero-sum. A made contract gives +2V to the declarer and -V to each defender (sum 0). A failed one gives -2V and +V, +V (sum 0).

Payoff table per deal (declarer / each defender):
| Contract | Made | Failed |
|---|---|---|
| 40 (V=1) | +2 / -1 | -2 / +1 |
| 50 (V=2) | +4 / -2 | -4 / +2 |
| 60 (V=4) | +8 / -4 | -8 / +4 |

How strong is the declarer? There is no talon, so the declarer holds only 1/3 of the cards. On average that is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 counting cards, about 27 card points. Choosing trump helps: the expected longest suit of 8 cards from 24 is about 3.3 of 6. Leading the first trick also helps. My rough estimate is that an average hand takes about 30-35 points. So 40 is made only with above-average hands, and 60 only with strong ones.

Thoughtless policies under the winner rule:
- Always 60: this player becomes declarer almost every deal (seat-order ties aside) and stakes -8 on mostly failing hands. Across 3 deals, sensible defenders who collect +4 per failure beat it. It loses.
- Always 40: it is outbid when others hold strong hands. When it does declare on weak hands, it averages a loss. It loses.
- Always PASS: as eldest, if both others pass (common, since they hold weak hands), it is forced to 40 with a random hand and usually takes -2. When others declare good hands and make them, it takes -V. It can lose a match, so it is not a never-lose policy.
- Random bidding loses to sensible bidding for the same reasons as always-60.

No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do. A higher bid only raises both the threshold and the stake.

Seat edge: within a deal, the eldest wins tie-breaks but also carries the forced-40 risk. Eldest rotates once per player over the 3 deals, so the match is symmetric. The declarer leads round 2, which offsets being outnumbered. All three players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete:
- Deal, simultaneous bid poll, tie-break by seat order from the eldest, and the all-pass default to eldest at 40 are all specified.
- Trump choice is specified.
- Legal-card rules are specified: follow suit and beat if able unless the trick is trumped; else trump and over-trump if able; else play anything.
- Trick winner, scoring, and the winner/draw rule are specified.

The one reading needed, that you must still play a trump even when you cannot beat the trump already played, follows from 'must play a trump'.

The game is finite (27 rounds) and decided by arithmetic on the match scores.

Against the limits:
- rounds 27 ≤ 40
- choice steps 3 ≤ 4 (bid poll + trump in round 1; three sequential card plays in rounds 2-9)
- one shuffle per deal ≤ 1
- the three private hands fit hidden_hands
- attributes: 3 hands, 3 trick cards, led suit, leader, trump, declarer, V/contract, declarer points, defender points, 3 match scores, eldest ≈ 17-18 ≤ 20
- 16 steps is tight, because rank lookups and the legal-card filter cost extra steps, but it fits under 20, and the legal-card check can be a referee rule check.

No board, clock or binding agreement is needed. Simultaneous bidding is correctly a poll, and card play is legitimately sequential.

No talk is a sensible choice for 3 players. Defenders want the same outcome, so talk there would only be signalling that the first speaker dictates. The repeated-game betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance dominates.

There are only 3 deals, so a match has only 3 bidding decisions and 3 trump choices. The result of each deal turns mostly on hand strength.

Card play offers less choice than it seems. The must-follow, must-beat, must-trump and must-over-trump rules often leave 1-2 legal cards. Defenders must even overtake their own partner's winning card. Real choice is mostly limited to leads and to picking among the cards that beat the trick.

When every player plays well, each bids only on strong hands. With 8 random cards and no talon, roughly one player in a deal holds a biddable hand, or none does and the eldest is forced to 40. The player dealt the strongest hand(s) collects +2V to +8V; the others mostly pass and score ±V by the declarer's luck. If all three bid and play perfectly, the match winner is essentially whoever received the best hands in 3 deals.

Rough estimate: deal luck decides well over half of match outcomes, probably 60-70%. A skilled player cannot reliably beat a weaker one over a single 3-deal sample. There is something to infer: the bids, and inference from forced plays. But too few independent decisions exist to overcome the deal.

required_changes: Use duplicate dealing to remove hand luck. Shuffle once at the start, store the three 8-card hands, and in deals 2 and 3 rotate the same hands so every player holds each hand exactly once, with eldest rotating as now. This still uses at most 1 random draw per round, and 27 rounds.
Alternatively, or as well, raise the number of independent deals to 4 (36 rounds ≤ 40) so skill has more decisions to show itself.

Give card play more real choice. Drop the requirement to beat a card already played by your own partner (or the must-beat rule for defenders entirely), so defenders choose between overtaking and discarding a low card. This makes play and inference matter more than forced sequences.

Optionally add a 2-card talon dealt face down, which the declarer picks up and then discards 2. Contracts then reward hand evaluation in bidding rather than raw deal strength; this is within hidden_elements ≤ 3.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFFS: Every deal is zero-sum. The declarer gets +2V or -2V, and each defender gets -V or +V. V is 1, 2 or 4 for a 40, 50 or 60 contract, doubled for Hearts trump and doubled again for Flek, so V can reach 16. If the declarer makes the contract with probability p, the declarer's expected gain is 2V(2p-1), and each defender's is -V(2p-1). Declaring pays only when p > 0.5. Flek scales both outcomes symmetrically, so defenders should Flek exactly when they believe p < 0.5. No option is strictly better whatever the others do.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule):
(1) ALWAYS 60 and Hearts. The declarer must take 60 of 90 points. A random 8-card hand of 24 holds on average 80/3 ≈ 27 Ace/Ten points. The contract is rarely made, roughly p ≈ 0.1-0.2. EV per deal won at auction is about 2*8*(2*0.15-1) ≈ -11, and about -22 once defenders Flek. It also wins the auction almost every deal, because nobody else bids 60 with an ordinary hand. Against sensible and against random opponents it ends last almost every match.
(2) ALWAYS PASS. If everyone passes, nobody scores. Otherwise the passer is always a defender. Sensible players declare only when p > 0.5, so the passer's expected result is -V(2p-1) < 0 on each such deal. Sensible play then ends ahead, so this policy loses.
(3) ALWAYS 40. It becomes declarer whenever the others pass, including with weak hands where p < 0.5. Defenders Flek those deals, so its EV is negative. It loses to sensible play. Against random play the result varies and does not reliably win.
(4) ALWAYS FLEK. This doubles the stakes on contracts sensible declarers chose because they expect to make them. Flekking a sensible declarer is therefore negative EV, and the policy loses.
No policy wins or draws almost every time.

SEATS: The eldest only breaks bid ties, and each seat is eldest exactly once. Each seat holds each of H1, H2 and H3 exactly once (duplicate rotation). The declarer always leads, whatever their seat. No seat gets a systematic edge from move order. All three players can realistically win. Equal-skill play tends toward near-equal totals or draws, which is acceptable.

ARITHMETIC CHECK: 8 Aces and Tens × 10 = 80, plus 10 for the last trick = 90. This matches the stated total.

playable.evidence:
(1) RULE GAP WHEN TRUMP IS LED. The overtaking duty for the led suit applies only 'if no trump has been played in this trick'. When trump is led, a trump has by definition been played. Read literally, a player holding trumps never has to beat the highest trump in a trump-led trick, though they must head a non-trump lead. This contradicts the stated intent ('must head the trick') and the original game. Models and the referee will rule it differently.

(2) COMPLEXITY UNDERCOUNTED. The engine's step list is flat, so the round-1 steps and the trick steps must sit in one list, each gated by `when` conditions.
Round-1 steps (about 13):
- deal-1 shuffle and store
- deal-2 draw and rotation
- deal-3 assignment
- bid poll
- highest bid with tie-break by seat from the eldest (about 2-3 calc steps)
- all-pass check
- trump choice
- announcement
- Flek poll
- V calculation (base, Hearts, Flek)
- announcement
Trick-round steps (about 7-8):
- sequential play
- legality check
- trick winner
- point award
- last-trick bonus
- leader update
- scoring at round 9 (made/failed: 2-3 steps)
This comes to about 21-24 steps, above the cap of 20, not the 16 declared.
Attributes are also over 20 once fully listed: H1-H3 (3), current hands (3), scores (3), bids (3), declarer, trump, contract, V, two Flek choices, declarer points, defender points, current trick cards/leader, deal index and the draw result.
Choice steps reach exactly 4 (bid, trump, Flek, trick play) only if one sequential step covers all three card plays. The design does not say so.

(3) THE HIDDEN-INFORMATION CLAIMS ARE INACCURATE. After deal 1 is played, all 24 cards have been shown publicly with their players. In deal 2 every player knows all three hands; the 50/50 draw hides only which opponent holds which, and the first trick reveals it. Deal 3 is fully determined, since it is the other derangement, and is perfect information. 'Each player's hand is private' and hidden_elements=2 overstate what is hidden. The rules should state this explicitly, or the design should change.

WHAT IS ADEQUATE:
- The game is finite (27 rounds) and decided by arithmetic.
- One random draw per round is respected.
- There is no board, clock or trading.
- No talk is a sensible choice for a trick-taking game. Defenders signal through card play, and open talk would let them coordinate trivially.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
DUPLICATE ROTATION: Every player holds each of H1, H2 and H3 once, so the main luck in card games, who gets the strong hand, is largely cancelled.

LUCK THAT REMAINS:
- Which hand sits to whose left in deal 2 (a 50/50 draw), which affects defender positions.
- In deal 1, everyone has to infer the unseen 16 cards.
- When every player follows the intended good strategy (bid only when p > 0.5, Flek only when p < 0.5), the same hand produces about the same contract and result whoever holds it. Players finish close or draw. The draw does not alone decide the winner.
- I estimate chance accounts for roughly 15-25% of the result, mainly the deal-1 inference and the deal-2 seat orientation.

WHAT SKILL DECIDES: Bid sizing, trump choice, Flek judgement and card play under following and trumping duties. Deals 2-3 become largely calculation with near-perfect information, which still rewards reasoning. Deal 1 offers real inference: unseen hands, and reading opponents' bids and Flek decisions. A strong player is clearly favoured. The design would be stronger with more hidden information in deals 2-3 (see playable).

required_changes: Fix the trump-led case. State: 'If you hold the suit led and your opponent's card is currently winning, you must beat it if you can with a card of that suit (this applies also when trump is led); if a non-trump suit was led and a trump has already been played, any card of the led suit is legal.'

Recount and declare the full flat step list with `when` gates for round 1 and for rounds 2-9, keeping it at or below 20. For example: precompute the deal-2 and deal-3 hand assignments in deal 1 so each later deal needs one assignment step; compute V in one calc step; do the tie-break in one calc step.

Give an explicit attribute list at or below 20. For example, use engine hidden_hands for the current hands instead of attributes, and drop the per-seat bid attributes by computing the winning bid directly from the poll.
State that all three card plays in a trick use one sequential choice step, so choice_steps_per_round stays at 4.

Remove or correct the claim that hands are private in deals 2-3. Either state openly that after deal 1 the hands are public knowledge (and declare hidden_elements accordingly), or keep information hidden: for example, leave 2 cards undealt as a hidden talon of 22 dealt cards (7/7/8, or 8/7/7 with the declarer taking the talon), so the rotated hands are not fully known.

balanced.evidence:
Scoring is zero-sum. Made: declarer +2V, each defender -V. Failed: declarer -2V, each defender +V. Stake table: 40 gives V=1 (+2/-2); 50 gives V=2 (+4/-4); 60 gives V=4 (+8/-8). Hearts trump or a Flek doubles V, and both together quadruple it, so a 60 in Hearts with Flek risks 32.

Card points: 8 Aces and Tens make 80, plus the last trick 10, for 90. About 1 of the 8 Aces/Tens is expected in the 3-card talon (3/24 x 8 = 1). The declarer holds 7 of the 21 live cards (33%) against two defenders with 14.
- A 40 contract needs about 44% of the points. It is makeable with a strong trump holding, for example A-10-K of trump plus side Aces: those cards alone hold 40 or more and win most of their tricks.
- A 60 contract needs about 67% of the points and is rarely makeable.
- The stake gradient therefore rewards accurate hand evaluation.

Thoughtless policies under the winner rule:
(1) Always PASS. This player is never declarer and takes the defender result. Sensible opponents bid only on strong hands and usually make them, so the passer loses V per made contract. Against sensible play it finishes below a bidder who makes contracts, so it loses. Against random bidders, who often overbid and fail, it gains. If all three always pass, every player has 0 and the game is drawn. It neither always wins nor never loses.
(2) Always bid 60. This player wins nearly every auction: a tie at 60 goes to the lowest score, then to seat order. It fails most contracts at -8 to -32 each, so it loses to both sensible and random play.
(3) Always 40. This player becomes declarer on weak hands whenever others pass or tie, fails often at -2V, and loses to sensible play.
(4) Always FLEK. This doubles the stake both ways, so it costs the defender when contracts are made. It is not dominant.
(5) Always NO. This gives up value against overbidders. It is not dominant.

No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do.

Seat effects: the declarer leads, and play then follows seat order. 'Eldest' matters only as the second tie-break for equal top bids at equal score. Seats 1 and 2 are eldest twice and Seat 3 once, which is a minor asymmetry. The first tie-break, lowest score, is a catch-up rule.

All three seats can realistically win. No labelled payoff ordering is contradicted by the numbers.

playable.evidence:
The rules cover every situation:
- Dealing: 7/7/7 to the players and 3 to the talon.
- Bid options: PASS, 40, 50, 60, made in one simultaneous poll.
- All-pass: the deal is skipped using a when-condition on each step. This needs no block selection.
- Tie-breaks for the declarer.
- Trump choice.
- Flek, as a simultaneous poll of the two defenders.
- V arithmetic.
- Lead and play order.
- Legal-card rules: follow suit, beat the winning card of the suit led, otherwise trump and overtrump, otherwise any card. These are a complex rule check the referee model can rule on.
- Trick winner, point pooling, last-trick bonus, and contract scoring.

The game is finite (40 rounds: 5 deals of 1 bidding round plus 7 tricks with 7-card hands) and the winner is decided by arithmetic on match scores, with ties drawn.

Complexity is within limits:
- One random draw per round (the shuffle in round 1 of each deal).
- Hidden elements: hands and talon, 2 of 3.
- Rounds: 40.
- Steps: 19 is plausible for a flat, when-gated list with dealing done by remove/append.
- Choice steps: 4 (bid poll, trump, Flek poll, trick play as one sequential choice from the leader) is consistent.

No board, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed.

No talk is correct here. Any table talk would be public, so it would inform the declarer as much as the partner. Defenders signal through card play, as in the original. Bidding is a sealed simultaneous poll.

Late rounds: in the final deal a leader cannot hide by passing. Trailing players can bid and so force the leader to defend at risk, so there is no safe option that wins every late round.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The deal decides who holds strong hands, and with only 5 deals this luck is substantial. I estimate 40-50% of outcomes between equally skilled players are driven by hand strength.

However, the decisive choices depend on skill:
- Bid evaluation against unknown hands and a hidden talon that may hold about 10 card points.
- Choosing a contract level against the 2:4:8 stake gradient.
- Flek as a read on the declarer's bid.
- Seven tricks of play with forced follow and overtrump rules. Here players infer voids and trump counts from the cards played, and defenders coordinate silently.

A defender with a weak hand can still gain V by defeating a contract, so a bad deal can be overcome.

Under all-good play, contracts are bid only when makeable. The result then depends on the quality of card play and defence as well as the deal, so it is not decided by the draw alone.

Against a careless player, who overbids, fleks badly or misplays tricks, a reasoning player is clearly favoured, because each mistake swings 2V to 4V. There is hidden information to infer (hands, talon, partner's holding) and a means to act on it (bids, Flek, card choice).
